thread.title: Alex Jones and InfoWars Are Just the Latest Episode of the Same Social Media Conundrum

author: Jon Swartz
title: Alex Jones and InfoWars Are Just the Latest Episode of the Same Social Media Conundrum
text:
Alex Jones of InfoWars Illustration: Sean P. Anderson By Jon Swartz Aug. 10, 2018 4:31 p.m. ET With every passing week, the social-media world is dealing with a new crisis of confidence and identity. This week’s topic was how to handle the hate-mongering from Alex Jones’ InfoWars.
After allowing the InfoWars controversy to fester for months, Apple (ticker: AAPL), Spotify (SPOT), Facebook (FB), and Google’s YouTube finally cracked down by removing his commentary from their platforms. Twitter (TWTR) has yet to make a similar move. CEO Jack Dorsey tweeted, “[T]he reason is simple: He hasn’t violated our rules.”
But there’s nothing simple about social media these days. After months of questions around data privacy, and election meddling, Facebook, Twitter et al. are now making decisions about speech. They haven’t handled the task particularly well, but then, freedom of speech is a topic that our country has been struggling with for 250 years.
Profit-driven companies are being asked to make public-safety-driven decisions. That’s not to let corporations off the hook. Facebook has amassed two billion-plus users, so it has no choice but to think like the most public of entities.
And investors must decide what that means for stock prices and private valuations. Twitter’s Dorsey previously has made a big deal about cleaning up the service’s user base, and the company’s stock has been punished in the process. Perhaps that has made Dorsey skittish about how to handle Jones .
Before Jones, tensions were already high—highlighted by Facebook’s late-July announcement that it had identified and shut down a shadowy, covert influence campaign with 290,000 followers that spent $11,000 on 150 ads over the past year. Facebook didn’t identify the culprits, but members of Congress—namely, Sen. Mark Warner (D., Va.)—and U.S. intelligence officers say similarities in intent and methodology point squarely at Russia.
Related Reading
Jack Dorsey Is a Double-Duty CEO for Twitter and Square. Here’s How He Revived Them Both. How Some CEOs Successfully Run More Than One Company The latest disclosure comes at a precarious time for Facebook, whose chief security officer, Alex Stamos, long rumored to be on the way out, announced on Aug. 1 that he was leaving to join Stanford University as a teacher and researcher. (Nonetheless, Stamos co-hosted the recent election-tampering announcement, just one day before confirming his departure.)
The stakes are particularly high, with fewer than 90 days until the U.S. midterm elections. But the threat will linger well beyond the vote. “I have no confidence they are ahead of the problem,” Brian Wieser, an analyst at Pivotal Research Group who has long been bearish on Facebook, tells Barron’s .
Future disclosures—or the countermeasures that Facebook is taking to stop them—are likely to crunch Facebook’s stock again.
“It’s nearly impossible to quantify operating costs,” Wieser says. “The whole notion of platform safety goes far beyond elections, which includes content moderation, content expenses, and platform improvement. I mean, it’s a good sign Facebook is doing things, but they have been so slow to respond.”
Daniel Ives, head of technology research at GBH Insights, is among those analysts who have recalibrated the way they assess Facebook stock and its earnings multiple. In addition to poring over numbers for monthly active users, advertising revenue, and operating margins, Wall Street is evaluating security costs and “silver bullet” issues that could crop up between now and Nov. 6. Facebook and Twitter are lined up to report in late October.
Trillium Asset Management, which holds 50,000 Facebook shares, isn’t sure the social-networking giant can “address the issue successfully,” but is satisfied that it has factored in “some error in what it would cost,” says Jonas Kron, director of shareholder advocacy at Trillium.
On Facebook’s earnings call last month, CEO Mark Zuckerberg cautioned, “We are investing so much on security, it will significantly impact profitability.” His company is now talking about future operating profit margins in the mid-30% range, down from the current 44%.
Investors have punished Twitter, as well. The stock fell 20% after it reported a decline in monthly active users, to 335 million, for its fiscal second quarter and warned of more to come as it attempts to rid itself of fake and suspicious accounts. A silver lining: Twitter’s revenue rose 24% year over year, and revenue per user grew 20% from the level a year earlier.
Cybersecurity experts—and the companies themselves—are bracing for more threats in what Facebook Chief Operating Officer Sheryl Sandberg frequently calls an “arms race.”
Newsletter Sign-up Twitter’s massive cleanup “merely took out the lowest of the low-hanging fruit,” warns Jonathon Morgan, founder of nonprofit Data For Democracy, which has criticized social media’s impact on elections. He maintains that Facebook, Twitter, Reddit, and Instagram remain vulnerable to disinformation because it doesn’t take many bots or people to influence small pockets of voters. “You can eliminate millions of bots around celebrities, but that doesn’t stop determined political activists,” he warns. “Facebook and Twitter face the same threat in 2018 as they did in 2016.”
Maybe worse. Security experts caution that attacks have become more sophisticated and are metastasizing—18 countries had some sort of social-media or electronic meddling in the past year, says Theresa Payton, the White House chief information officer under President George W. Bush and current CEO of security-consulting company Fortalice Solutions.
“We don’t think that this work will necessarily ever be done,” Dorsey said of Twitter’s expunging efforts on a recent conference call with investors. “It doesn’t have an endpoint.”
